what_its_for: Enalaprilat is a medicine given through an IV (intravenous line) in a hospital or clinic to lower high blood pressure quickly. It belongs to a group of medicines called ACE inhibitors, which help relax and widen your blood vessels so your heart does not have to work as hard.
how_to_take: This medicine is given to you by a nurse or doctor directly into your vein through an IV line. You will not take this medicine by mouth at home. Your healthcare team will monitor you closely during and after each dose to check your blood pressure and make sure you are safe.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your blood pressure, kidney function, and other medicines you are taking. A typical dose is 1.25 mg given slowly into your vein over at least 5 minutes, every 6 hours as needed. People with kidney problems or those who also take water pills (diuretics) may receive a lower starting dose of 0.625 mg. Only your healthcare team will adjust your dose — never try to change it yourself.
missed_dose: Because this medicine is given by healthcare professionals in a medical setting, your team will manage your dosing schedule. If you have any concerns about your treatment schedule, ask your nurse or doctor right away.
storage: You do not need to store this medicine at home. It is kept and prepared by hospital or clinic staff. For reference, the medicine should be stored at room temperature away from light, and once mixed, it should be used within 24 hours.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor or nurse before receiving this medicine if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant — it can seriously harm an unborn baby. Avoid potassium supplements or salt substitutes containing potassium unless your doctor approves, as this medicine can raise potassium levels. Let your healthcare team know about all other medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take, especially water pills, other blood pressure medicines, or NSAIDs like ibuprofen or naproxen.
when_to_call_doctor: Tell your nurse or doctor right away if you notice any of the following during or after receiving this medicine: sudden swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat (this is called angioedema and is a serious reaction); severe dizziness or fainting; very low blood pressure symptoms like lightheadedness when you stand up; decreased urination or signs of kidney problems; chest pain; or any signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, itching, or difficulty breathing.
when_it_works: This medicine starts working within 15 minutes of being given into your vein. Your blood pressure should begin to drop within 15 to 30 minutes, and the effect usually lasts about 6 hours. Your healthcare team will monitor your blood pressure throughout your treatment.
special_populations: Pregnant women should NOT receive this medicine, especially during the second and third trimesters, as it can cause serious harm or death to the unborn baby. Breastfeeding mothers should talk to their doctor about risks. Older adults and people with kidney disease may need lower doses and extra monitoring because the medicine stays in the body longer. Children may receive this medicine in carefully adjusted doses as determined by their doctor.
